metadata.note: godot-gamedev + walker teardown of Bao Xing's CSYE 7270 shader assignment. Every code panel is a verbatim excerpt of godot/ at 4246f94bd3db51c0644ecc3bef9b3a8c8427911b (read with git show, never the working tree); the gameplay shot is a real Movie Maker capture of an isolated copy of that revision, driven through the real input map by the disclosed capture driver; controlled-value captures, material captures and the film's shader-pair fixture are labelled as such. No paid call, no upload.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude composer; reconstructed Walker prompt from Bao's CHANGE-BRIEF.md (not a recorded session). Liam introduces himself.
beats.narration_text: Ciao, this is Liam, in for Bear. Bao Xing's shader assignment for Lanternfall: write a shader from code that shows a game state, give a 3D object a textured shader, and answer four questions about shaders, materials, textures and Godot's shading language, each one pointing at a line of Bao's own code. Here's the ask, rebuilt from Bao's change brief.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about Lanternfall, a lamp-headed courier surviving three minutes in a fog-bound night market, into two Godot 4 shaders: a yellow tint that shows his 48-tick protection after a hit, and a textured cobblestone material for the 3D room. Gameplay must not change. Predict every colour by hand first, then measure it in the engine.

beats.narration_text: What the assignment asks for, and how Bao answered it. A shader from code that communicates a state: here, the courier turns yellow after an accepted hit and fades back as his forty-eight ticks of protection run out. A textured shader on a 3D object: the floor and the stand-in of the Assignment 3 room. Four questions, each answered at a line of code. And tests, with an honest list of what they can't show.

props.title: What the assignment asks
props.excerpt: The courier turns yellow after an accepted hit, then gradually returns to its incoming colour as protection expires. This communicates temporary invulnerability and gives the player a visible warning that the next collision will soon cause damage again. It confirms an actual damage event rather than merely proximity to an enemy. The existing red blink continues to signal the hit; the yellow tint shows the remaining protection.

beats.narration_text: Before any code ran, Bao's brief fixed the colour line and worked out the answers by hand. The line mixes the incoming colour toward yellow by hurt amount: at zero the drawing passes through, at one it's yellow. Halfway, the lamp head should land at two forty-eight point five, two nineteen point five, thirty-seven point five, and the coat at one fifty point five, one fifty-six point five, forty-four point five. In the red blink the same mix keeps more red. And two point oh, set from code, should not be clamped.

beats.narration_text: Here's Bao's hand-written shader, all nine lines. Line one makes it a canvas item shader, for 2D sprites. Line four declares hurt amount, the one number the game sends in; its hint range only shapes the Inspector slider. Then fragment, on line seven, runs for every pixel the courier covers, and line eight is the whole effect: the incoming colour, mixed toward yellow. That's what a shader does: a small function, run for every pixel.

beats.role_note: Code beat (code-then-result-v1): godot/effects/hurt_tint_presentation.gd lines 18-30 at 4246f94, read verbatim; the next beat shows the result.
beats.narration_text: The driver connects the game to that uniform. Every frame, line twenty-two calls refresh. Line twenty-six turns the courier's remaining invulnerability ticks into a fraction: forty-eight ticks is one, zero is zero, clamped. Outside playing, paused or the level-up screen, it's forced to zero, so a lethal hit can't leave him yellow. And line thirty sets the shader parameter. The driver only reads the game; it never writes it.

beats.narration_text: Now the running game, with scripted input through the real input map. A monster connects, and the courier is yellow at once. The script presses pause, and the tint holds at twenty-three forty-eighths, because the counter stops with the simulation. Resume, and it drains. On the next hit a monster keeps touching him while he's protected, and nothing restarts. Frame by frame: one to zero in forty-eight ticks, eight tenths of a second, with the red blink still showing through.

beats.role_note: Code beat (code-then-result-v1): godot/a5/materials/cobblestone_warm_floor.tres lines 8-18 at 4246f94, read verbatim; the next beat shows the result.
beats.narration_text: So what's a material? This file. Line ten points at the shader. Lines eleven to thirteen hand it the three maps. And lines fourteen to eighteen are just values: a warm tint, the map repeated twice, a matte roughness range. The stand-in's file points at the same shader with different values: cooler, larger, shinier. The shader is the code; each material is a set of numbers for it.

beats.role_note: Code beat (code-then-result-v1): godot/shaders/cobblestone_surface.gdshader lines 17-24 at 4246f94, read verbatim; the next beat shows the result.
beats.narration_text: Now the shader side, Bao's fragment function. Line eighteen scales the u v coordinates. Line nineteen samples the colour map and multiplies by the tint: that's the albedo. Line twenty-one hands the normal map to the engine. And line twenty-two is Bao's latest edit: the relief's depth is scaled by how squarely the surface faces the camera, half strength edge-on, full strength face-on.

beats.narration_text: Change the shader instead, and both objects move. An earlier Codex run made a similar edit, turning both green, and broke the rule that agents never touch Bao's shaders.

beats.role_note: Code beat (code-then-result-v1): godot/shaders/cobblestone_surface.gdshader lines 1-5 at 4246f94, read verbatim; the next beat shows the result.
beats.narration_text: Why is a texture information? Because the same kind of file can hold three kinds of data, and only the hint tells the engine which. Line three marks the colour map source color: these bytes are colour. Line four marks the normal map hint normal: these are directions. Line five, roughness, has no colour hint at all: raw numbers. And line one, shader type spatial, puts all of it in the 3D pipeline.

beats.narration_text: Here are the three files: colour, a purple-blue map of directions, and grey numbers. A map of directions can be checked like data. This normal map's curl ratio is zero point two two in the OpenGL convention and one point seven eight read as DirectX, and the DirectX calibration file is its mirror image, so it's a real surface in the right convention. And on the floor, normal strength zero against one changes how the stone joints are shaded.

beats.narration_text: The sweep moves each of those five numbers, one at a time, on the floor only: low, the material's own value, then high. Through all fifteen captures the stand-in never moves. Bao's look at the new normal strength row: at zero, the surface is flatter and the normal relief is off; at one, the stone edges and joints look more three-dimensional; at two, stronger light and dark relief, deeper joints, an exaggerated bump.

beats.role_note: Result of B21. Verbatim lines from godot/ at 4246f94; agent-made film fixture capture/shader_pair_fixture.gd rendered on an isolated copy (not gameplay, values set in memory); measurements by tools/pair_diff.py.
beats.narration_text: Lined up: generated line seven against Bao's line three, nineteen against four, thirty-five against nineteen. Different names, same jobs. To see whether they draw the same, this film rendered both on the same plane under one light, as a labelled fixture. Face-on, about nine pixels in ten agree within two levels of two fifty-five. beats.narration_text: So, the four questions, each at a line. What a shader does: hurt tint line eight, a function run for every fragment. How a material differs from a shader: one shader, two material files of values. Why a texture is information: lines three to five say colour, directions, or raw numbers. beats.narration_text: The tests drive the real game. This run places one wraith twenty pixels away, presses a real Enter key to start, waits for a real contact to land, then holds W to walk away. A sampler that runs after everything else records the uniform every frame. The test never calls the driver or sets the value itself.
